opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so what I find really interesting there is that with a recurrent-depth model you basically get speculative decoding almost for free. In standard speculative decoding you need two models: a small, fast draft model that proposes a few tokens, and the large model that verifies them in parallel. Getting those two to agree well is a whole engineering problem. You have to train or pick a draft model, keep both in memory, and make sure their distributions line up well enough that you actually accept a good fraction of the drafts.

With a recurrent architecture, where you have a block of layers you can iterate as many times as you want at test time, the draft model and the full model are the same model. You just run fewer iterations of the recurrent block to draft. A shallow pass with only a few recurrences gives you a cheap guess at the next couple of tokens, and then you verify with the full number of iterations. There are no extra parameters and no second model to train. It's the same weights, just a different amount of compute.

What makes it more than a trick, to me, is what it says about the model. It suggests that the early iterations already land in roughly the right region of latent space, and the later iterations are refining. For a lot of tokens, the easy ones like finishing a word or some boilerplate, the model has basically converged after a few steps, so the cheap draft and the expensive verifier agree. On the harder tokens they disagree, and that's exactly where you want to spend the extra compute. So speculative decoding becomes a way of exploiting the fact that the model has adaptive compute built in.

It also connects to other things you can do with these models, like per-token adaptive exits, where you stop iterating once the latent state stops changing, or reusing the KV cache across iterations. All of these are inference-time tricks that a fixed-depth transformer can't easily do, and they come from the same property: depth is a knob you can turn at test time, not something baked in when you trained the model. That's a big part of why I think recurrent depth is a promising direction.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the draft and full verifier are the same recurrent model, using fewer recurrences to draft and the full number to verify.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something that fell out of the recurrent-depth work almost by accident, and I think it's one of the more fun consequences of the architecture. The basic idea with the recurrent-depth model is that instead of stacking, say, 64 distinct layers, you have a small prelude, a core block of layers that you loop over some number of times, and then a coda that decodes to the output. The number of loops is a knob you set at inference time. More loops, more compute per token, and for a lot of tasks the model's answer gets better as you iterate.

What's interesting for speculative decoding is that this gives you a draft model and a verifier model for free, and they're literally the same weights. Normally, if you want to do speculative decoding, you have to go find or train a separate small model that approximates the big one, and you worry about whether its distribution is close enough, whether the tokenizer matches, whether you've got the memory for two sets of parameters. Here, you just run the core with a small number of recurrences, say four or eight, to produce a few draft tokens cheaply, and then you verify them by running the same model with the full recurrence depth, thirty-two or whatever your target is. The KV cache is shared, the embeddings are shared, everything lines up by construction.

And there's a subtler thing I find kind of elegant, which is that the draft isn't just a worse model that happens to agree sometimes. The early iterations are quite literally the first steps of the computation the full model is going to do anyway. So in a sense the verifier can pick up where the drafter left off, rather than starting from scratch. We haven't squeezed everything out of that yet, but the intuition is that the state after eight iterations is already most of the way to the state after thirty-two for easy tokens, and only the hard tokens really need the extra depth.

Which is the other part I like: this connects to the adaptive compute story. Easy tokens, the ones where the latent state converges quickly, are exactly the tokens where the shallow draft will be accepted. Hard tokens are where the draft gets rejected and the full-depth model does its work. So speculative decoding becomes a fairly natural mechanism for spending compute where the model actually needs it, without having to train a separate exit classifier or anything like that. You get a per-token compute allocation almost as a side effect of a standard inference trick. That's the kind of thing that makes me think the recurrent view is a good way to organize these models, beyond just the parameter-efficiency argument.

r001.rationale: It explains that the same model drafts with a small number of recurrences and verifies with its full recurrence depth.

astra-6.text:
What I find interesting is that you can potentially use the same model both to draft tokens and to verify them. With speculative decoding, you normally have a small model that proposes a few tokens, and then a larger model checks those proposals. That works well, but now you have two models to manage, and you need the small model to agree with the large one often enough to make it worthwhile.

With a recurrent transformer, you have another way to vary the amount of computation: you can run fewer recurrent steps to get a cheap prediction, or more steps to get a more expensive prediction. So you could imagine using a shallow recurrence to draft, and then using the full recurrence to verify.

The interesting question is whether those cheaper predictions are close enough to the full computation to give you a useful acceptance rate. Sharing weights doesn't automatically guarantee that. But it gives you a very natural setting for exploring this tradeoff between how much computation you spend drafting and how much work you save during verification.

r001.rationale: The response says the same recurrent transformer can draft with a shallow/fewer recurrence and verify with the full recurrence.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find interesting is that you can potentially use the same model for both drafting and verification. In speculative decoding, you usually have a small model propose a few tokens, and then a larger model checks them. That works well, but now you have two models to manage, and their predictions need to agree often enough for you to get a speedup.

With a recurrent transformer, you reuse the same block of layers for multiple iterations. So you can imagine running fewer iterations to produce a cheap draft, then using more iterations to verify it. The draft and the verifier share parameters, which makes this a pretty natural way to vary how much computation you spend.

The interesting question is whether the predictions at that lower compute budget are close enough to the predictions after more iterations. Sharing weights doesn't guarantee that. But if they are, you have a way to turn the model's ability to think for different amounts of time into an inference speedup.

r001.rationale: It says the same recurrent transformer can produce a cheap draft with fewer iterations and verify it with more iterations.
